subject: ss
title: Economics in History and Geography: Industry, Labor, Trade, Maps, and Migration
objectives: Students will explain how industrialization changed work, cities, and the U.S. economy, and identify causes and effects in economic history.
Students will describe why workers formed labor unions and how government responded to labor problems.
Students will use opportunity cost and comparative advantage to explain specialization and trade, and describe the effects of tariffs.
Students will locate places using latitude and longitude on a coordinate grid and identify hemispheres and directions.
Students will apply the five themes of geography, including regions, human-environment interaction, and push and pull factors in migration.
teach:
Objectives

  • Explain how industrialization changed work, cities, and the U.S. economy, and trace cause-and-effect chains in economic history.
  • Describe why workers formed labor unions and how government responded.
  • Use opportunity cost and comparative advantage to explain trade, and describe the effects of tariffs.
  • Locate places by latitude and longitude on a grid and name hemispheres and directions.
  • Apply the five themes of geography, especially regions, human-environment interaction, and migration.

Materials

  • Student Lesson (printed or on screen) and the study sheet (Notes)
  • Whiteboard or shared screen with a blank grid drawn from −6 to 6 on both axes
  • Week 8 Social Studies practice set (12 items)

60-Minute Plan

SegmentMinutesWhat happens
Warm-up5"Why do people move?" discussion and three quick questions
Direct instruction20Industrialization and labor; trade; maps and coordinates; themes of geography and migration; worked examples
Guided practice15Four questions worked together, including a grid task
Independent practice15Practice set items 1–8 (finish 9–12 at home)
Wrap-up5Checks for understanding and exit ticket from the Post Lesson

Warm-up (5 minutes)

Ask: "Think of someone you know who moved to a new town or country. What made them leave? What drew them to the new place?" List answers in two columns, Reasons to leave and Reasons to go. Tell students they have just listed push and pull factors. Then ask:

  1. Name one item in this room that was made in a factory. Answer: almost anything (clothing, a phone, a chair). Before about 1800, most goods like these were made by hand.
  2. Which imaginary line divides Earth into the Northern and Southern Hemispheres? Answer: the equator (0° latitude).
  3. What is a tax on imported goods called? Answer: a tariff.

Direct Instruction (20 minutes)

A. Industrialization (5 minutes)

  • Industrialization is the shift from hand production to machine production in factories. It began in Great Britain in the late 1700s with cotton textiles and steam power.
  • It reached the United States around 1790, when Samuel Slater, a British-trained mechanic, helped start a water-powered cotton-spinning mill in Pawtucket, Rhode Island. Beginning in the 1820s, mills in Lowell, Massachusetts, hired young women from New England farms; by the 1830s thousands worked there.
  • Transportation drove growth. The Erie Canal (1825) linked the Hudson River at Albany to Lake Erie at Buffalo and sharply cut shipping costs. The first transcontinental railroad was completed at Promontory Summit, Utah, in 1869.
  • After the Civil War, steel (Andrew Carnegie) and oil (John D. Rockefeller) became giant industries. The Sherman Antitrust Act (1890) outlawed combinations that restrained trade.
  • People followed the jobs to cities: about 20% of Americans were urban in 1860, and the 1920 census was the first to count more than half (51.2%) as urban.

B. Labor (4 minutes)

  • Factory work often meant 10- to 12-hour days, six days a week, low pay, child labor, and dangerous machines. One worker alone had little power to bargain.
  • Workers formed labor unions to bargain as a group (collective bargaining) and sometimes went on strike. The American Federation of Labor (AFL), led by Samuel Gompers, was founded in 1886. Strikes such as the Pullman Strike (1894) were often broken with court orders or troops.
  • The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire in New York City (March 25, 1911) killed 146 workers, many of them young immigrant women; some exit doors were locked. New York passed new safety laws afterward.
  • New Deal laws: the National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act, 1935) protected the right to unionize; the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938) set a federal minimum wage of 25 cents an hour, required overtime pay beyond a standard workweek (44 hours at first, 40 by 1940), and restricted child labor.

C. Trade (4 minutes)

  • Exports are sold to other countries; imports are bought from them. Imports greater than exports = trade deficit; exports greater = trade surplus.
  • Absolute advantage: producing more with the same resources. Comparative advantage: producing at a lower opportunity cost. David Ricardo explained this idea in 1817. Even a country that is better at everything gains by specializing in what it gives up the least to make, and trading.
  • A tariff taxes imports, a quota limits them, and an embargo bans trade with a country. Tariffs protect some domestic producers but raise consumer prices. After the Smoot-Hawley Tariff (1930) raised U.S. tariffs sharply, other countries retaliated and world trade shrank during the Depression. NAFTA (1994) lowered barriers among the United States, Canada, and Mexico; the USMCA replaced it in 2020.

D. Maps, latitude, and longitude (4 minutes)

  • Map parts: title, legend (key), compass rose, scale, and grid. Map types: political (borders, cities), physical (landforms, water), and thematic (one topic, such as rainfall). Every flat map distorts something: on a Mercator map, Greenland looks about as big as Africa, though Africa is roughly 14 times larger.
  • Latitude lines run east-west and measure distance north or south of the equator (0° to 90°). Longitude lines run pole to pole and measure distance east or west of the prime meridian through Greenwich, England (0° to 180°).
  • Write latitude first, with direction letters: New Orleans is at about 30°N, 90°W. Board trick: latitude lines are like the rungs of a ladder ("ladder-tude"); longitude lines are long, pole to pole.

E. Themes of geography and migration (3 minutes)

  • Five themes: location (absolute = coordinates; relative = near what), place, human-environment interaction, movement, and region.
  • Regions: formal (a shared measurable feature, such as a climate zone), functional (organized around a hub, such as a city's delivery area), perceptual (based on people's feelings, such as "the Heartland").
  • Human-environment interaction: people depend on, adapt to, and modify the environment. Hoover Dam (completed 1936) modified the Colorado River for water and power. In the Dust Bowl of the 1930s, farmers had plowed up the grasses that held Great Plains soil; when drought struck, the soil blew away and many families left.
  • Migration: push factors drive people out (war, famine, persecution); pull factors attract them (jobs, freedom, family). Migration can be forced (the Atlantic slave trade; the Cherokee Trail of Tears, 1838–1839). In the Great Migration (about 1910–1970), roughly 6 million African Americans left the rural South for cities in the North, Midwest, and West.

Worked examples (model each one aloud)

Example 1: Reading coordinates. On a grid, the horizontal axis is the equator and the vertical axis is the prime meridian; each line is 1°. A town is 3 units left of the prime meridian and 5 units above the equator. Give its coordinates and hemispheres.

Solution: Up means north: latitude 5°N. Left means west: longitude 3°W. Latitude first: 5°N, 3°W, in the Northern and Western Hemispheres. Stress the common error of writing "3°N, 5°W" by reading across first, as with (x, y) in math.

Example 2: Comparative advantage. In one hour, Ana can bake 4 pies or 8 loaves of bread. Ben can bake 1 pie or 4 loaves. Who should bake which?

Solution: Ana is faster at both (absolute advantage in both). Compare opportunity costs.

  • 1 pie costs Ana 8 ÷ 4 = 2 loaves; it costs Ben 4 ÷ 1 = 4 loaves. Ana has the comparative advantage in pies.
  • 1 loaf costs Ana 4 ÷ 8 = 1/2 pie; it costs Ben 1 ÷ 4 = 1/4 pie. Ben has the comparative advantage in bread.

Both gain if Ana specializes in pies, Ben in bread, and they trade.

Example 3: Cause and effect. "After the Erie Canal opened in 1825, goods moved by boat between Lake Erie and the Hudson River much more cheaply than before." What effect would you expect on New York City?

Solution: Model the chain on the board: canal → lower shipping costs → more trade through New York's port → business and population growth. GED cause-and-effect questions usually test one link of a chain like this.

Example 4: Push or pull? Classify each reason for the Great Migration: (a) segregation laws in the South; (b) factory jobs in Detroit and Chicago during World War I; (c) the boll weevil destroying Southern cotton crops.

Solution: (a) push; (b) pull; (c) push. Test: "Is this about the old place or the new place?"

Guided Practice (15 minutes)

Work these together. Draw the grid for item 1 and have students point before they answer.

  1. A city is plotted 5 units right of the prime meridian and 1 unit below the equator. Give its coordinates. Answer: 1°S, 5°E (latitude first, not 5°S, 1°E).
  2. Country X can make 10 bikes or 5 tents per worker per day. Country Y can make 6 bikes or 6 tents. Which has the comparative advantage in tents? Answer: Country Y. A tent costs X 10 ÷ 5 = 2 bikes but costs Y only 6 ÷ 6 = 1 bike.
  3. A city builds levees to keep a river from flooding. Which part of human-environment interaction is this? Answer: modifying the environment.
  4. A new tariff raises the price of imported steel. Who most likely benefits, and who is hurt? Answer: domestic steel producers and their workers benefit; buyers of steel, such as car makers and builders, pay more.

Independent Practice (15 minutes)

Students complete practice items 1–8 on their own. Circulate and ask, "Where on the grid or in the text did you find that?" Items 9–12 can be finished at home.

Checks for Understanding

  • "Which comes first in coordinates?" Expected: latitude (N or S), then longitude (E or W).
  • "Absolute vs. comparative advantage?" Expected: absolute = producing more; comparative = lower opportunity cost.
  • "Give one push and one pull factor." Expected: a reason to leave (war, drought) and a reason to go (jobs, family).
  • "Name one law that responded to workers' problems." Expected: the Wagner Act (1935), the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938), or New York's safety laws after the Triangle fire.

Common Mistakes and How to Correct Them

Reversing latitude and longitude. Students used to (x, y) read across first. Repeat "latitude first" and make them say the direction letter every time: a coordinate marked N or S is always latitude.

Confusing absolute and comparative advantage. Students assume whoever makes more should make it. Require them to compute what is given up before answering.

Ignoring the human part of human-environment interaction. A drought alone is a natural event. It becomes human-environment interaction when people's actions (plowing grassland) or responses (migrating, planting windbreaks) are involved.

Percentage points vs. percent. A rise from 20% to 40% is 20 percentage points (a 100% increase). GED items usually ask for the simple difference in points.

Differentiation

Support: Give students a printed grid labeled N (top), S (bottom), E (right), and W (left), and have them label the four quadrants (NE, NW, SE, SW) first. For trade problems, provide a table with the column "To make 1 of this, I give up ___."

Stretch: Have students write a paragraph linking three topics, for example: the transcontinental railroad (industrialization) opened Plains markets (trade), encouraging wheat farming that later contributed to the Dust Bowl (human-environment interaction) and migration west. Label each link as a cause or an effect.

How This Shows Up on the GED

Economics and geography each make up about 15% of the GED Social Studies test, and many history questions carry economic content. Expect:

  • A map described as a grid or table: "Which city is located at…?" or "In which direction would a traveler go?"
  • A historical line or bar graph: "Which statement is supported by the graph?" or a fill-in asking for a difference
  • A production table: "Which country has a comparative advantage in…?"
  • A short reading: "Which was a cause of…?" or "Which details support…? Select two."
  • Drag-and-drop sorting (push vs. pull) and drop-down sentences that complete a statement with the correct term

Tell students: on map questions, say the direction letters out loud; on trade questions, find what is given up, not just what is made.
student:
Why This Matters

About 15% of the GED Social Studies test is economics and about 15% is geography. Many history questions also ask about money, work, and trade. This week you will connect three big stories (factories, workers, and trade) and learn the map skills you need to read any geography question.

1. Industrialization: From Hand-Made to Machine-Made

Industrialization is the change from making goods by hand to making them with machines in factories. It began in Great Britain in the late 1700s and reached the United States around 1790, when the first successful water-powered cotton-spinning mill opened in Rhode Island. Starting in the 1820s, large textile mills in Lowell, Massachusetts, hired young women from New England farms. By the 1830s, thousands worked there.

Better transportation helped factories sell goods farther away:

  • Erie Canal (1825): connected the Great Lakes to New York City by water and made shipping much cheaper.
  • Transcontinental railroad (1869): linked the East and West coasts by rail.

Factories needed workers, so people moved from farms to cities. In 1860, about 1 in 5 Americans lived in an urban area. By 1920, more than half did.

2. Labor: Workers Organize

Early factory jobs often meant 10 to 12 hours a day, six days a week, low pay, child labor, and dangerous machines. One worker alone had almost no power to demand better treatment, so workers formed labor unions. A union bargains with employers for the whole group (collective bargaining). If talks fail, workers may go on strike (refuse to work).

In 1911, a fire at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York City killed 146 workers, many of them young immigrant women. Some exit doors had been locked. Public anger led to new safety laws. Later, in the 1930s, federal laws protected workers' right to join unions (1935) and set a minimum wage, overtime pay, and limits on child labor (Fair Labor Standards Act, 1938).

3. Trade: Why Countries Buy and Sell

Exports are goods a country sells to other countries. Imports are goods it buys from them. Countries trade because of specialization: each one focuses on what it produces best.

Opportunity cost = what you give up to make something.
Absolute advantage = you can make more of it.
Comparative advantage = you give up less to make it (lower opportunity cost).
Countries should specialize in what they have a comparative advantage in, then trade.

Worked example 1. In one week, a worker in Alta can make 20 shirts or 10 radios. A worker in Bora can make 12 shirts or 4 radios. Which country has the comparative advantage in radios?

Step 1: Find what each country gives up to make 1 radio. Alta: 20 ÷ 10 = 2 shirts. Bora: 12 ÷ 4 = 3 shirts.
Step 2: The lower cost wins. Alta gives up only 2 shirts.
Answer: Alta has the comparative advantage in radios. (Bora has it in shirts: a shirt costs Bora 1/3 of a radio but costs Alta 1/2 of a radio.)

Governments sometimes limit trade. A tariff is a tax on imports. It helps businesses at home that compete with the imports, but it usually raises prices for shoppers. A quota limits how much can be imported, and an embargo stops trade with a country completely. Free trade agreements, such as the one among the United States, Canada, and Mexico, lower these barriers.

4. Reading Maps

Check these parts first on any map:

  • Title: what the map is about.
  • Legend (key): what the symbols and colors mean.
  • Compass rose: north, south, east, and west.
  • Scale: how map distance compares to real distance (for example, 1 inch = 50 miles).

A political map shows borders and cities. A physical map shows mountains, rivers, and other landforms. A thematic map shows one topic, such as rainfall or population.

5. Latitude and Longitude

Mapmakers use a grid of imaginary lines to give every place an exact address.

LatitudeLongitude
MeasuresDistance north or south of the equatorDistance east or west of the prime meridian
Starting line (0°)EquatorPrime meridian (through Greenwich, England)
Range0° to 90° N or S0° to 180° E or W
Memory trickLike the rungs of a ladder ("ladder-tude")Lines are long, pole to pole

Rule: Write latitude first, then longitude, and always include the direction letters. New Orleans is at about 30°N, 90°W.

On the GED, a map may be shown as a simple grid. Read it like this: the horizontal line through the middle is the equator, and the vertical line is the prime meridian. Up is north, down is south, right is east, left is west.

Worked example 2. On a grid where each line is 1°, a town sits 5 lines to the left of the prime meridian and 3 lines above the equator. What are its coordinates?

Step 1: Latitude: 3 lines above the equator = 3°N.
Step 2: Longitude: 5 lines left of the prime meridian = 5°W.
Answer: 3°N, 5°W. (Not 5°N, 3°W: latitude always comes first.) The town is in the Northern and Western Hemispheres.

6. Five Themes of Geography

  1. Location: where a place is. Absolute location is exact (coordinates). Relative location describes a place by what is near it ("just south of the river").
  2. Place: what a place is like (its land, climate, people, and culture).
  3. Human-environment interaction: how people depend on, adapt to, and change their environment.
  4. Movement: how people, goods, and ideas travel.
  5. Region: an area with something in common, such as climate, language, or crops.

A famous example of human-environment interaction is the Dust Bowl of the 1930s. Farmers on the southern Great Plains had plowed up the deep-rooted grasses that held the soil in place. When a long drought hit, strong winds blew the dry soil away in huge dust storms. Many farm families lost everything and moved west to California.

7. Migration: Push and Pull

Migration is moving to a new home. People leave because of push factors and choose a destination because of pull factors.

Push (reasons to leave)

  • War or violence
  • Famine or drought
  • Persecution or unfair laws
  • No jobs

Pull (reasons to go)

  • Jobs and higher wages
  • Safety and freedom
  • Family already there
  • Available land

Worked example 3. Between about 1910 and 1970, roughly 6 million African Americans moved from the rural South to cities in the North, Midwest, and West. This is called the Great Migration. Is "segregation laws in the South" a push or a pull factor?

Step 1: Ask: Is it about the old place or the new place? It describes the South, the place people left.
Answer: Push factor. (Factory jobs in Chicago or Detroit would be pull factors.)

Try It

1. A city on a grid is 5 lines below the equator and 1 line to the right of the prime meridian. Write its coordinates.

Show answer

5°S, 1°E. Below the equator is south, right of the prime meridian is east, and latitude is written first.

2. A worker in Country P can make 8 tables or 4 boats. A worker in Country Q can make 3 tables or 3 boats. Which country has the comparative advantage in boats?

Show answer

Country Q. A boat costs P 8 ÷ 4 = 2 tables, but costs Q only 3 ÷ 3 = 1 table. Q gives up less.

3. A government places a 25% tariff on imported cars. What will most likely happen to the price shoppers pay for imported cars?

Show answer

It will most likely rise, because the tax on imports raises the cost of bringing the cars into the country, and sellers pass that cost on to buyers.

4. Farmers in a dry area dig canals to bring river water to their fields. Which theme of geography does this show?

Show answer

Human-environment interaction. The farmers are changing (modifying) the environment to meet their needs.

5. A family leaves its home country because a war has destroyed their town. Is the war a push or a pull factor?

Show answer

A push factor. It is a reason to leave the old place.
post:
Summary of Key Points

  • Industrialization moved production from homes and shops to machine-powered factories. Canals and railroads widened markets, and people moved to cities: the 1920 census was the first to count more than half of Americans as urban.
  • Long hours, low pay, child labor, and danger led workers to form unions and bargain collectively. Government responded with safety laws after the 1911 Triangle fire, the Wagner Act (1935), and the Fair Labor Standards Act (1938).
  • Countries trade because of specialization. A country should produce what it has a comparative advantage in, meaning the lowest opportunity cost, even if another country can produce more of everything.
  • A tariff taxes imports, helping some producers at home but raising prices for consumers.
  • Latitude measures north-south from the equator; longitude measures east-west from the prime meridian. Write latitude first.
  • The five themes are location, place, human-environment interaction, movement, and region. Migration is driven by push factors (reasons to leave) and pull factors (reasons to go).

Exit Ticket

1. A town on a grid is 6 lines above the equator and 1 line to the left of the prime meridian. What are its coordinates?

Show answer

6°N, 1°W.

2. What is the difference between an import and an export?

Show answer

An import is bought from another country; an export is sold to another country.

3. Name one reason factory workers formed labor unions in the late 1800s.

Show answer

To bargain as a group for higher wages, shorter hours, or safer conditions, because one worker alone had little power.

4. Building a dam to create a reservoir is an example of which kind of human-environment interaction: depending, adapting, or modifying?

Show answer

Modifying. People are changing the environment.

5. During the Great Migration, were wartime factory jobs in Northern cities a push factor or a pull factor?

Show answer

A pull factor. They attracted people to the new place.

Reflection

  • Think about the work your family has done over three generations. How does that history show changes in the economy, such as a move from farm to factory to service jobs?
  • Which was harder for you this week: reading coordinates or figuring out comparative advantage? What step tripped you up?
  • Choose one migration you know about (your own family's or a historical one). List one push factor and one pull factor.

Test-Taking Strategy: Say the Direction Out Loud

On any map or grid question, touch the point and say its directions out loud (or in your head): "two up, so 2 north; four left, so 4 west." Then check your answer choice for both the numbers and the letters. Most wrong answers on coordinate questions have the right numbers with the wrong letters, or the numbers in the wrong order.

vocab.def: Talks between a union and an employer about wages, hours, and working conditions.
vocab.example: After weeks of collective bargaining, the workers won a 5% raise.

vocab.def: A refusal by workers to work until their demands are met.
vocab.example: The railroad workers went on strike when their wages were cut.

vocab.def: What you give up when you choose to use resources for one thing instead of another.
vocab.example: If a worker makes 1 pie instead of 2 loaves of bread, the opportunity cost of the pie is 2 loaves.

vocab.def: The ability to produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than someone else.
vocab.example: Bora has a comparative advantage in shirts because it gives up fewer radios to make each shirt.

vocab.def: A tax on goods imported from another country.
vocab.example: A tariff on imported steel raised the price of steel for car makers.

vocab.def: An export is a good sold to another country; an import is a good bought from another country.
vocab.example: The United States exports soybeans and imports coffee.

vocab.def: Distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees from 0° to 90°.
vocab.example: A city at 30°N is 30 degrees north of the equator.

vocab.def: Distance east or west of the prime meridian, measured in degrees from 0° to 180°.
vocab.example: A city at 90°W is 90 degrees west of the prime meridian.

vocab.def: An area that shares one or more features, such as climate, language, landforms, or economic activity.
vocab.example: The Great Plains is a region of flat grassland used for farming and ranching.

vocab.def: The ways people depend on, adapt to, and change their natural surroundings.
vocab.example: Building a dam to store water for a desert city is human-environment interaction.

vocab.def: The movement of people from one place to another to live.
vocab.example: During the Great Migration, millions of African Americans moved from the rural South to Northern cities.

vocab.def: Push factors are reasons people leave a place; pull factors are reasons they move to a new place.
vocab.example: A drought (push) and factory jobs in a city (pull) can both lead a farm family to move.

stimuli.title: Reading: Factories, Workers, and Reform
stimuli.html:
(1) In the early 1800s, most Americans worked on farms or in small shops. Over the next hundred years, machines powered first by water and later by steam and electricity moved much of the nation's production into large factories. Factories could make cloth, shoes, and steel far more cheaply than skilled workers could by hand, and prices for many goods fell.

(2) For workers, however, the change came with a cost. A typical factory employee in the late 1800s worked 10 to 12 hours a day, six days a week. Children, many of them younger than 14, tended machines in textile mills and sorted coal in mines. Machines had few safety guards, and workers who lost fingers or hands in accidents usually received no payment from their employers.

(3) Because one worker could easily be replaced, many workers decided that they had a better chance of winning higher pay and safer conditions if they acted together. They formed labor unions, which bargained with employers on behalf of all their members. The American Federation of Labor, founded in 1886, became the largest union organization of its time. When bargaining failed, unions sometimes called strikes.

(4) Public opinion began to shift after a disaster in New York City. On March 25, 1911, a fire broke out at the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory. Some exit doors had been locked, and 146 workers, most of them young immigrant women, died. New York State soon passed dozens of new fire-safety and workplace laws.

(5) The federal government acted during the Great Depression. The National Labor Relations Act of 1935 protected workers' right to form unions. The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set a national minimum wage, required overtime pay for long workweeks, and restricted child labor.

stimuli.title: Reading: The Dust Bowl
stimuli.html:
The southern Great Plains, including parts of Oklahoma, Texas, Kansas, Colorado, and New Mexico, was once covered by deep-rooted prairie grasses. These grasses held the soil in place through dry spells and strong winds.

In the 1910s and 1920s, high wheat prices and new gasoline-powered tractors encouraged farmers to plow millions of acres of this grassland and plant wheat. For several years, rainfall was good and harvests were large.

Then, in the early 1930s, a severe drought struck. With the grass gone and the crops dying, nothing held the dry topsoil. Strong winds lifted it into enormous dust storms. On April 14, 1935, remembered as "Black Sunday," a wall of dust swept across the region and turned day into night.

Many families lost their farms. Hundreds of thousands of people left the Plains, many heading west to California in search of farm work. In 1935, Congress created the Soil Conservation Service, which taught farmers to plant windbreaks of trees, rotate crops, and plow along the curves of the land to hold the soil.

items.skill: Cause and effect in economic history
items.prompt: According to the passage, why did many workers form labor unions?
options: Acting as a group gave them a better chance of winning higher pay and safer conditions.
The federal government required every factory worker to join a union.
Factory owners asked workers to organize so production would increase.
Unions helped workers find jobs on farms instead of in factories.
items.hint: Paragraph 3 begins with the word "Because." Read that sentence closely.
items.explain:
Paragraph 3 says that "because one worker could easily be replaced, many workers decided that they had a better chance of winning higher pay and safer conditions if they acted together." That is the reason unions formed.

The passage never says the government required union membership. The 1935 law in paragraph 5 protected the right to form unions, which is different. Nothing in the passage says owners asked workers to organize or that unions sent workers back to farms.

items.prompt: Which town on Kestrel Island is located at 2°N, 4°W?
options: Port Alder
Fairview
Dunmore
Brightwater
items.hint: Latitude comes first. Go 2 lines up from the equator, then 4 lines left of the prime meridian.
items.explain:
Step 1: 2°N means 2 lines above the equator.
Step 2: 4°W means 4 lines left of the prime meridian.
Step 3: The town at that point (−4, 2 on the grid) is Port Alder.

Fairview is at 4°N, 2°W; choosing it means the numbers were reversed (reading across first, as in an (x, y) math graph). Dunmore is at 2°S, 4°E, which has the right numbers but the opposite directions.

items.prompt: Drag each reason for migrating into the correct category.
choices: A drought destroys the crops on a family's farm.
Factory jobs in a growing city pay higher wages.
The government jails people for practicing their religion.
A country offers free farmland to new settlers.
Relatives already living in the new country can help newcomers find housing.
A war breaks out in the family's home region.
items.hint: Ask: Is this a problem with the place people are leaving, or an attraction of the place they are going?
items.explain:
Push factors (problems in the old place): drought destroying crops, religious persecution, and war.

Pull factors (attractions of the new place): higher-paying factory jobs, free farmland, and relatives who can help. Note that the relatives are a pull factor even though they are family: they make the new place more attractive.

items.prompt: Which statement is supported by the graph?
options: 1920 is the first census year shown in which more than half of the U.S. population lived in urban areas.
The urban share of the population fell during at least one ten-year period shown.
By 1880, most Americans lived in urban areas.
The urban share grew by the largest amount between 1870 and 1880.
items.hint: Look for the first point on the line that is above 50%. Then check each ten-year change.
items.explain:
The values are 19.8, 25.7, 28.2, 35.1, 39.6, 45.6, and 51.2. Only 1920 (51.2%) is above 50%, so 1920 is the first year shown with an urban majority.

The line rises every decade, so it never fell. In 1880 only 28.2% lived in urban areas, far less than half. The 1870–1880 increase (28.2 − 25.7 = 2.5 points) was actually the smallest; the largest was 1880–1890 (35.1 − 28.2 = 6.9 points).

items.prompt: By how many percentage points did the urban share of the U.S. population increase from 1860 to 1920?
items.hint: Subtract the 1860 value from the 1920 value.
items.explain:
1920 value: 51.2%
1860 value: 19.8%
Change: 51.2 − 19.8 = 31.4 percentage points.

A common error is subtracting the wrong year, such as 51.2 − 25.7 = 25.5 (using 1870 instead of 1860).

items.prompt:
Surveyors plan to dig a new well on Kestrel Island at 4°S, 1°W. Click the point on the grid where the well will be located.

(On the grid, the horizontal axis is the equator and the vertical axis is the prime meridian. Each line is 1 degree.)
items.hint: Start where the axes cross. South means down; west means left.
items.explain:
Step 1: 4°S is latitude, so move 4 lines down from the equator.
Step 2: 1°W is longitude, so move 1 line left of the prime meridian.
Step 3: The well is at the grid point (−1, −4).

Clicking (−4, −1) reverses latitude and longitude; that point would be 1°S, 4°W. Clicking (1, −4) uses east instead of west.

items.prompt:
Complete the statements.

Hoover Dam, completed in 1936, blocks the Colorado River to store water and produce electricity for cities and farms in the Southwest. Building the dam is an example of the geography theme {{0}}.

Geographers mapped every county in which more than half of the farmland is planted in corn. The area made up of those counties is an example of a {{1}}, because it is defined by a shared, measurable feature.

options: human-environment interaction
movement
relative location
place
formal region
functional region
perceptual region

items.hint: For the first blank, ask whether people are changing nature. For the second, ask how the region's boundary was drawn.
items.explain:
Blank 1: human-environment interaction. Damming a river is people modifying the environment to meet their needs for water and power. "Movement" might seem tempting because water and electricity travel to cities, but the key action described is changing the river itself.

Blank 2: formal region. A formal region is defined by a feature that can be measured and is shared across the area (here, more than half the farmland in corn). A functional region is organized around a central hub, such as a city's delivery area, and a perceptual region is based on people's opinions or feelings about an area.

items.prompt: Based on the table, which country has a comparative advantage in producing cloth, and why?
options: Sudia, because it gives up 1 bushel of wheat for each bolt of cloth, while Norland gives up 2 bushels.
Norland, because one Norland worker can make more cloth per day than one Sudia worker.
Norland, because it gives up only 1/2 bolt of cloth for each bushel of wheat.
Sudia, because it produces the same amount of wheat and cloth.
items.hint: Find the opportunity cost of 1 bolt of cloth in each country: how much wheat is given up?
items.explain:
Norland: 6 wheat or 3 cloth, so 1 cloth costs 6 ÷ 3 = 2 bushels of wheat.
Sudia: 2 wheat or 2 cloth, so 1 cloth costs 2 ÷ 2 = 1 bushel of wheat.
Sudia gives up less wheat for each bolt of cloth, so Sudia has the comparative advantage in cloth.

Norland makes more cloth (3 vs. 2), but that is an absolute advantage, not a comparative one. The third choice describes Norland's opportunity cost of wheat, which shows Norland's comparative advantage is in wheat, not cloth. The last choice states a fact from the table but does not give a valid reason.

items.prompt: Which details from the passage support the claim that factory work in the late 1800s and early 1900s could be physically dangerous? Select two answers.
options: Machines had few safety guards, and workers lost fingers or hands in accidents.
Some exit doors had been locked, and 146 workers died in the Triangle fire.
The American Federation of Labor was founded in 1886.
Factories could make cloth, shoes, and steel more cheaply than skilled workers could.
The Fair Labor Standards Act of 1938 set a national minimum wage.
A typical factory employee worked six days a week.
items.hint: Look for details about injuries or deaths, not about pay, hours, or laws.
items.explain:
The claim is about physical danger. Two details show it directly: machines without safety guards that cost workers fingers and hands (paragraph 2), and locked doors that contributed to 146 deaths in the Triangle fire (paragraph 4).

A six-day workweek shows the work was long and tiring, but it does not show injury or death. The AFL's founding, cheaper factory goods, and the minimum wage law are true details from the passage but do not describe danger.

items.prompt: Which statement best describes the relationship between people and the environment shown in the passage?
options: People changed the land by removing its grass cover; when drought came, the damaged land forced many people to move away.
The drought alone caused the dust storms, and farming practices played no part.
Farmers moved to the Plains because dust storms had already made the soil richer.
The government's soil programs caused the drought by changing how farmers plowed.
items.hint: Find two things in the passage: something people did to the land, and something the land then did to people.
items.explain:
The passage describes a two-way chain. First, people modified the environment: farmers plowed up the deep-rooted grasses that held the soil (paragraph 2). Then the changed environment affected people: during the drought, nothing held the soil, dust storms followed, and many families lost their farms and migrated west (paragraphs 3–4).

The drought was a natural cause, but the passage clearly says "with the grass gone… nothing held the dry topsoil," so it is wrong to say farming played no part. The soil programs came after the dust storms (1935), so they could not have caused the drought of the early 1930s.

items.skill: Direction and hemispheres on a map grid
items.prompt: A small plane flies in a straight line from Dunmore to Port Alder. Which statement accurately describes the flight?
options: The plane flies northwest and crosses both the equator and the prime meridian.
The plane flies northwest and crosses only the equator.
The plane flies northeast and crosses both the equator and the prime meridian.
The plane flies southwest and crosses only the prime meridian.
items.hint: Write the coordinates of both towns first. Did the latitude change from S to N? Did the longitude change from E to W?
items.explain:
Step 1: Dunmore is at 2°S, 4°E. Port Alder is at 2°N, 4°W.
Step 2: Direction: going from south to north is moving north; going from east to west is moving west. Together that is northwest.
Step 3: Lines crossed: latitude changes from south to north, so the plane crosses the equator. Longitude changes from east to west, so it also crosses the prime meridian.

"Northeast" comes from mixing up east and west (Port Alder is to the left, which is west). "Crosses only the equator" ignores the change from E to W longitude.

items.prompt: Which conclusion about trade between Norland and Sudia is best supported by the table?
options: Both countries can gain if Norland specializes in wheat, Sudia specializes in cloth, and they trade.
Norland cannot gain from trade, because its workers produce more of both goods than Sudia's workers.
Sudia should specialize in wheat, because it gives up less cloth to grow wheat than Norland does.
Only Sudia can gain from trade, because it is the less productive country.
items.hint: Find each country's opportunity cost for both goods. Each country should make the good it gives up the least to produce.
items.explain:
Opportunity cost of 1 bushel of wheat: Norland gives up 3 ÷ 6 = 1/2 bolt of cloth; Sudia gives up 2 ÷ 2 = 1 bolt. Norland's cost is lower, so Norland has the comparative advantage in wheat.
Opportunity cost of 1 bolt of cloth: Norland gives up 2 bushels; Sudia gives up 1 bushel. Sudia has the comparative advantage in cloth.

When each country specializes in its comparative advantage and trades, both can end up with more than they could make alone. The idea that Norland cannot gain because it is better at both goods is the classic misconception that comparative advantage disproves: absolute advantage does not decide who gains. The third choice is wrong because Sudia gives up more cloth (1 bolt) than Norland (1/2 bolt) to grow a bushel of wheat.
